nameStory: The 'cellophane-cuckoo' name comes from this bee's sneaky lifestyle - like a cuckoo bird laying eggs in other birds' nests, these bees slip into the nests of cellophane bees to lay their own eggs. The 'notch-backed' part refers to a distinctive indentation or groove on the back portion of their body that helps separate them from their cuckoo bee cousins.
description: The Notch-backed Cellophane-cuckoo Bee is a small, sleek parasitic bee that doesn't build its own nest or collect pollen. Instead, it sneaks into the underground nests of cellophane bees (also called plasterer bees) to lay its eggs, leaving the host to raise its young. These bees have a somewhat wasp-like appearance with their smooth, sparsely-haired bodies and distinctive white or pale yellow bands across their dark abdomen. They're typically about 1/4 to 1/2 inch long and have a more streamlined look than the fuzzy bees they parasitize.

idTips.label: Notched Back
idTips.description: Look for a distinctive groove or indentation on the back section (scutellum) - this notch is the key feature that gives this species its name and separates it from other cuckoo bees

idTips.label: Banded Abdomen
idTips.description: The dark abdomen has pale yellowish or white bands that look almost painted on, creating a clean striped pattern unlike the fuzzy, pollen-dusted bands of worker bees

idTips.label: Smooth Body
idTips.description: The body feels and looks much smoother than typical bees, with sparse, short hairs rather than the dense fuzz of pollen-collecting species

idTips.label: Wasp-like Appearance
idTips.description: At first glance resembles a small wasp with its sleek build and relatively hairless appearance, but closer inspection reveals the broader head typical of bees

idTips.label: Ground-level Activity
idTips.description: Often seen flying low over sandy or bare ground areas where their host cellophane bees nest, with a searching, somewhat erratic flight pattern

habitat: Look for these bees in areas where their cellophane bee hosts nest - typically sandy soils, bare patches in lawns, walking paths, and sunny slopes with well-drained ground. They're often found in residential areas, parks, and edges of fields where the soil has been disturbed or compacted. You'll spot them flying low over the ground, searching for host nests to infiltrate.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge and begin seeking host nests, appearing as early cellophane bees start their nesting activities. Look for them flying close to the ground in sunny, warm weather.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most commonly observed searching for and infiltrating cellophane bee nests. This is the best time for identification and observation.
seasonality.fall: Activity winds down as the life cycle completes and new adults prepare to overwinter. Late-season individuals may still be visible on warm days.
seasonality.winter: Adults overwinter in protected locations like leaf litter or soil crevices, remaining inactive and hidden until spring warmth triggers emergence.

funFact: These bee 'pirates' have evolved to be so perfectly synchronized with their hosts that they can smell the exact chemical signature of a freshly provisioned cellophane bee nest, allowing them to time their break-ins to the moment when the host has just stocked the nest with food but hasn't yet sealed it shut!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with small wasps due to their smooth, relatively hairless bodies and wasp-like flight pattern. Remember: bees have broader heads and slightly fuzzier bodies than wasps, and cuckoo bees are often seen hovering low over ground where bees nest, while wasps typically fly higher and visit flowers or hunt for insects.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'cuckoo bee' can be confusing since these aren't actually related to cuckoo birds - it's just a behavioral comparison. Also, despite being 'bad guys' that parasitize other bees, cuckoo bees are a natural part of the ecosystem and their presence actually indicates a healthy population of their host species.
compareHints: Among cellophane-cuckoo bees, the notched back is the key distinguishing feature of this species. The Two-banded Cellophane-cuckoo Bee has more prominent banding but lacks the distinctive notch, while the Dwarf and Least species are significantly smaller overall. Canadian Cellophane-cuckoo Bees tend to be more northern in distribution and have different band patterns.
